extracted.intended_audience: late-night TV viewers, fans of Conan O'Brien, and general readers interested in comedy/entertainment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit evaluation criteria for short, recurring comedy segments performed on late-night television, focusing on host buy-in, visual humor, rehearsal vetting, and audience resonance. Draws on examples from Conan O'Brien's tenure and his remarks about which bits he liked or disliked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host approval / buy-in
rubrics_metrics.description: The show's host must be willing to perform/own a bit; a lack of host approval undermines a segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conan repeatedly reads a pitched bit and says, 'No,' and would argue with writers ('I pay you guys? You get paid for this?'). If the host resists a bit it may be performed reluctantly (or the host will visibly try to 'kill' it), which affects audience perception and the segment's viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers' enthusiasm is not definitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers may become very excited about a concept, but their enthusiasm alone doesn't guarantee the bit will work on air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conan: '[My writers] would get really high on something ... And they showed it to me at rehearsal, and I went, “No.”' The piece notes writers argued Otis K. Dribbles was a hit even when the host doubted it: 'Writers aren't always correct.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual, cartoonish silliness
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong late-night bit can rely on a cartoonish, visually silly sensibility that creates immediate, broad laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conan: 'I’ve always had a very cartoonish sense of humor, and I like things to be visually silly.' Historical examples cited include The Masturbating Bear and Triumph the Insult Comic Dog, and Conan's preferred bits (Horse Riding a Horse, Shoeverine) emphasize visual absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must work silently / without sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Bits should be clear and funny even if the show's audio were turned off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conan: 'I always thought I want people to laugh at the show if the sound is off,' implying visual clarity and immediate gag readability are desirable traits for television bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal vetting and screening
rubrics_metrics.description: New bits are shown at rehearsal before being approved for broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conan describes writers showing segments at rehearsal and the host making a decision then ('they showed it to me at rehearsal, and I went, “No.”'). Rehearsal is a key opportunity to surface problems before airing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience resonance vs. creator taste
rubrics_metrics.description: A bit's success is judged by how it plays for the studio/audience and whether it resonates beyond creators' preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otis K. Dribbles 'appeared several times' because writers argued it was a hit, even though Conan remained doubtful; conversely, Conan's favorites sometimes 'didn’t resonate as much with his audience' (examples: Horse Riding a Horse, The Always Disappointing FedEx Pope, Shoeverine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring-segment viability
rubrics_metrics.description: Some bits can be repeated successfully as recurring segments, but recurrence doesn't equal quality if creators lack confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otis K. Dribbles became a recurring segment despite the host's misgivings; the article implies that repeatability and perceived 'hit' status by writers can drive recurrence even when other stakeholders disagree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of physical absurdism and costume/prop comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete absurd images (people in costumes, improbable bodily/comedic tableaux) are a common device for eliciting laughs on late-night TV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: 'a basset hound that's dressed like a minister, and he dribbles a basketball'; 'Horse Riding a Horse' (person in a horse costume riding a live horse); 'The Always Disappointing FedEx Pope' (man with a FedEx hat pretending to be the pope); 'Shoeverine' (Wolverine with shoes on his hands). These illustrate reliance on incongruous visual props and costumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-air signaling to 'kill' or distance from a bit
rubrics_metrics.description: Hosts may use visible reactions or off-camera behavior to indicate disapproval and attempt to stop a bit from landing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conan describes 'while they're doing it, I’m in the corner looking at the audience like…' and shaking his head 'Because the camera’s not on me, so I’m trying to kill it.' This technique affects audience reading and can be used to influence whether a bit succeeds.
